slides.title: Principle and place of the method
bullets: Sedimentation goes through three phases: first the red cells settle singly and slowly, then they form aggregates and settle fast, in the third phase the aggregates pack down and settling slows and stops.
ESR is not specific to any disease: it is used as a preliminary test and a screening test.

The Aripova book notes that ESR is not specific for finding acute and chronic diseases, is little used today and has been abandoned in many countries: age, pregnancy, the phase of the cycle and anaemia distort the result.
The international committee for standardisation and WHO recommend venous blood, an anticoagulant tube and a graduated vertical tube (the Westergren principle).

slides.title: Two described variants
rows: Capillary from the finger, or venous

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 1. Take the sodium citrate solution into a tube; add the blood to it at a ratio of 4:1 and mix well.
2. Draw the mixture into the graduated tube up to the 0 mark; check that the lower edge of the blood meniscus is at 0 and that there are no air bubbles.
3. Stand the tube upright in the rack (in the Panchenkov apparatus its lower end rests on rubber and the upper end is closed).
4. Leave the rack for one hour in a quiet place free of vibration and draughts.
5. After one hour measure in millimetres the distance from the 0 mark to the upper edge of the settled red-cell column — the height of the clear plasma layer.
6. Record the result in mm/h.

slides.title: Limitations and errors
bullets: ESR is not suitable when the red-cell count is reduced or the patient is dehydrated.
Physiological factors (age, pregnancy, phase of the menstrual cycle) and anaemia can give a wrong result.
The value may be raised in diseases that change the plasma protein pattern, chronic infection, normal pregnancy, tumours and tuberculosis.
The capillary-blood, 100 mm tube method used in laboratories of the former USSR should, where possible, be revised to meet international standards.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: In the standard method used in many countries blood may be spilled and aerosols may form, which is a considerable biological hazard.
The international committee for standardisation and WHO recommend single-use closed systems for ESR, so that the blood stays enclosed during testing and disposal.
